title: Scrolls, books and chapters
summary: The Hebrew Bible reckons twenty-four books, not thirty-nine: Samuel, Kings, Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah are each one book, and the twelve short prophets share one scroll. The Greek translators split Samuel and Kings into four books of Kingdoms and Chronicles into two, and Latin and English Bibles, and in time printed Hebrew ones, kept the splits. Chapters were added in the thirteenth century, verse numbers in the sixteenth.

hebrew.name: Torah
hebrew.summary: Five books, copied on one scroll with four blank lines between each; the Talmud still counts them as five of the twenty-four.

hebrew.name: Samuel
hebrew.summary: One book in Hebrew: Saul's death (1 Samuel 31) runs straight on into David hearing of it (2 Samuel 1). The Greek made it the first and second books of Kingdoms.

sources.title: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 6.25.2 (quoting Origen)
sources.note: 'the First and Second of Kings, among them one, Samouel'

hebrew.name: Kings
hebrew.summary: One book in Hebrew, whose break falls in the middle of Ahaziah's reign (1 Kings 22:51–2 Kings 1:18). The Greek made it the third and fourth books of Kingdoms.

sources.title: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 6.25.2 (quoting Origen)
sources.note: 'the Third and Fourth of Kings in one, Wammelch David'

hebrew.name: The Twelve
hebrew.summary: Twelve prophets on one scroll, counted as one book, with only three blank lines between them. The Talmud says why: Hosea written on its own, 'since it is small it would be lost'. Sirach already names them together as 'the twelve prophets'.

sources.title: Mur 88, the Minor Prophets scroll from Wadi Murabba'at
sources.note: one scroll holding Joel through Zechariah, 2nd century AD

hebrew.name: Ezra
hebrew.summary: One book in Hebrew, called Ezra; the Talmud asks why Nehemiah's words were not given a book of his own name. Origen counts 'Esdras, First and Second in one'.

sources.title: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 93b
sources.note: 'what is the reason that a book was not called by his name?'

hebrew.name: Chronicles
hebrew.summary: One book in Hebrew, Divrei haYamim, 'the events of the days', and the last of the Writings: the Hebrew Bible ends with Cyrus's decree. The Greek made it two books of Paraleipomena, 'things left out', and moved it after Kings.

sources.title: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 6.25.2 (quoting Origen)
sources.note: 'of the Chronicles, the First and Second in one, Dabreïamein'

overlaps.summary: Chronicles ends with the first words of Cyrus's decree, cut off at 'and may he go up', and Ezra opens with the same words and carries the sentence on: 'may he go to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD'. In the Hebrew order Ezra stands before Chronicles, so the repeated lines join the two books across the scroll's end.
traditions: Ezra wrote his own book and Chronicles' genealogies to his day: the Talmud (Bava Batra 15a)
One work by one writer, 'the Chronicler': Leopold Zunz (1832) and those who followed him
Two works by different hands, the repeated lines a link between them: Sara Japhet (1968), H. G. M. Williamson (1977)

numbering.label: Chapters
numbering.summary: Stephen Langton, teaching at Paris before he became Archbishop of Canterbury (d. 1228), divided the Latin Bible into the chapters still used, which passed into Greek, Hebrew and every modern Bible.

sources.title: Stephen Langton
sources.author: Catholic Encyclopedia
sources.note: 'he toted the Bible at Parys and marked the chapitres'

numbering.label: Verses
numbering.summary: Robert Estienne (Stephanus), a Paris printer, numbered the verses of the New Testament in his Greek edition of 1551, printed at Geneva; the numbers were later taken into whole Bibles.

sources.title: Estienne
sources.author: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed.
sources.note: 'In the Greek New Testament of 1551 (printed at Geneva) the present division into verses was introduced for the first time'
